name: Bell Beaker culture
title: The story of the Bell Beaker culture

text: About 4,800 years ago, people by the Tagus River in Portugal began making drinking cups shaped like an upside-down bell.
Archaeologists, people who dig up the past, call their way of life the Bell Beaker culture, after those cups.
src: come from the Tagus estuary in Portugal, radiocarbon dated to about the 28th century BCE / a drinking vessel shaped like an upside-down bell
The Bell Beaker culture is named after its most typical object

text: Beaker groups travelled by sea and along rivers, reaching the Rhine, Britain, Ireland and Hungary.
Later many Beaker people moved to Britain, and within a few hundred years most people there were descended from them.
src: Bell Beaker people travelled by sea and river / brought maritime beakers to the Lower Rhine about 2600 BCE / Beakers arrive in Britain and Ireland, and Bell Beaker groups reach Csepel Island in Hungary
the later spread was strongly linked to migration / In Britain it brought high levels of steppe-related ancestry and replaced about 90% of the gene pool within a few centuries

text: They were farmers who kept animals, grew barley and spun wool.
At Ross Island in Ireland they dug copper from the ground and made the first copper axes of Britain and Ireland.
src: mixed farming and animal husbandry / Pollen studies show more barley grown as beakers spread / spindles to the spinning of wool
At Ross Island in Ireland, the earliest known Irish copper mines, from about 2500 BCE, local ores were smelted into the first copper axes of Britain and Ireland

text: Later they used tin from Cornwall, in Britain, to make a new metal called bronze.
They also made ornaments and round discs of gold.
src: Tin from Cornwall and Devon was used to make bronze from about 2200 BCE / Britain became the first region of Europe to switch all its metalwork to tin-bronze
Gold was worked into lunulae, discs and ornaments

text: They often buried their dead one by one, curled up, with weapons beside them.
The Amesbury Archer, buried in the richest grave of his time in Britain, probably grew up near the Alps.
src: The typical Beaker burial was a single body, often crouched, under a mound and with weapons
Isotope analysis of the Amesbury Archer, the richest burial in Britain of his time (c. 2300 BCE), shows that he spent his childhood in Central Europe, probably in the region of the Alps.

text: When they came to Ireland, the old custom of building great stone tombs, like those at Knowth, came to an end.
Their beakers went out of use about 3,700 years ago, but their graves, mines and monuments remain.
src: In Ireland the arrival of the Beaker culture was accompanied by the destruction of smaller tombs at Knowth / marking the end of the Neolithic tradition of megalithic passage tombs
c. 1700 BCE: Beakers fall out of use in Britain and Ireland / Excavated graves, settlements, mines and monuments
